newsitem.title: USA: Former MGM chief skips sentencing hearing.
newsitem.headline: Former MGM chief skips sentencing hearing.

text.p: A lawyer for convicted former Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Inc. Chief Giancarlo Parretti asked a Delaware court to reschedule a sentencing hearing he missed on Monday because Parretti had to face fraud charges in Italy.
U.S. authorities, however, said Parretti left the United States illegally.

As a result Parretti could face an even stiffer sentence on his October 1996 perjury and jury-tampering conviction if he returns from Italy to face the sentencing judge, Deputy State Attorney General Paul Wallace said.
"I think this aggravates it even more," Wallace said. He said he had already been planning to ask for a "substantial jail time," for Parretti, who faced a term of up to 10 years.

Parretti, a flamboyant former hotel waiter who bought the fabled MGM studio in 1991 only to be ousted by his lender months later, surprised his U.S. lawyers last Friday by notifying them he was in Italy.

In response Delaware Superior Court Judge Richard Cooch on Friday canceled the sentencing hearing and issued a warrant for Parretti's arrest. He asked Wallace to suggest a new sentencing date by February 3.

On Monday Parretti's Italian attorney, Manlio Morcella, asked for postponement of the sentencing hearing "for five or six days" so Mr Parretti could hire a new lawyer and "bring some arguments to the attention of the (Delaware) court."
Cooch made no immediate ruling on Morcella's request.

Morcella earlier told the court Wallace agreed in October not to prosecute Parretti if Italian government actions prevented him from attending the sentencing. "I can declare that at the present time such actions exist," Morcella said.
Morcella told the court Parretti had to return to his native Italy to be present at an appeal on a 1990 bankruptcy fraud conviction. Parretti, 55, also is wanted in France.
But Wallace disputed Morcella's version of the October agreement.

"There was no agreement ... that he could leave the country to take care of Italian matters. Everyone understood that when bail was set in Delaware that he was not to leave the country," Wallace told Reuters.
He said Parretti could forfeit up to $125,000 in cash used to secure bail in Delaware and in California, where Parretti is fighting France's extradition request.

Parretti's Delaware conviction followed a 1991 civil lawsuit in the Delaware Chancery Court in which the French bank Credit Lyonnais won control of MGM, whose $1.3 billion purchase by Parretti it had helped to finance.

In documents released on Monday, Cooch ordered Parretti's U.S. attorneys, Eugene Maurer of Delaware and Jay Coggan of California, to report by January 21 on Parretti's departure and his plans to return to Delaware.
Cooch also denied a request by Coggan that he be excused from the case because his authority had been "revoked" by Parretti.
It is unknown when or how Parretti left the United States. A spokesman for the U.S. District Court in Los Angeles said that the court is still holding Parretti's passport.
